extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Coast Guard officers, federal acquisitions/contracting officers, OMB/agency policy analysts, and researchers studying OMB Circular A-76 implementation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and analysis of the Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76 implementation for U.S. Coast Guard commercial activities — assessing causes of post-award contract cost increases, cost‑effectiveness vs. the Government's Most Efficient Organization (MEO), and perceptions of the A-76 program among USCG leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost‑comparison principle (contracting vs. in‑house)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whenever an in‑house function can be performed by the commercial sector, a comparison of the cost of contracting and the cost of in‑house operation of the function will be made to determine who will do the work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central A‑76 evaluative rule: determine economy/productivity by direct cost comparison between contractor offers and the Government MEO cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of inherently governmental functions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Retain Governmental functions in‑house. Certain functions are inherently Governmental, not in competition with the commercial sector...and in the public interest, are required to be Government‑run.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions judged inherently governmental must be excluded from A‑76 contracting and retained in‑house; such classification is a gating criterion for whether to apply A‑76.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on commercial sector when economical
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Government is to rely on commercially available sources to provide commercial products and services. The Government will not start any commercial activity if the product or service can be provided more economically from a commercial source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy standard: prefer private provision when contracting yields lower evaluated cost; underpins choice to solicit competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/classification of 'Commercial Activities'
rubrics_metrics.description: A‑76 enumerates commercial activities (examples given: Food Services, Security, Transportation, Maintenance/Repair, Printing, ADP Services, Health Services, Office & Admin, Laundry, Real Property, Systems Engineering, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctly classifying an activity as 'commercial' (versus inherently governmental or exempt) is required before applying A‑76 procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) content and measurable standards
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The PWS is a Statement of Work (SOW) which contains the specifications that basically described what the function is and what it takes to do it.' The 1979 revision emphasized defining needs by measurable work standards, not on 'how' the activity was done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS must clearly specify required outcomes and measurable performance standards (not prescribe methods); PWS is the basis for solicitation and QA planning. Poorly written PWSs are cited as a source of problems/cost increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Assurance (QA) plan requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Quality Assurance (QA) plan for a possible service contract is developed within the PWS and 'is the action to be taken by the Government to ensure the goods and services received ... meet the requirement of the PWS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract evaluation and ongoing administration require a QA plan tied to PWS metrics; inadequate QA planning/implementation undermines contract outcomes and may contribute to cost increases or performance problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) standard and costing
rubrics_metrics.description: MEO is 'the best organizational structure and operating procedure for the function' and 'is intended to encourage efficiency by
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO must reflect the most efficient in‑house organization; its cost estimate is used in the sealed‑bid comparison and must be prepared rigorously — inaccurate MEO costing biases the contract/in‑house decision and subsequent savings calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10% personnel‑cost rule for award decision
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If the total cost of contracting out is less than the MEO's cost by more than 10 percent of the MEO's personnel related costs, and the offeror is determined to be responsible, then the commercial activity is contracted‑out. However, if the offeror's cost is within 10 percent of the MEO cost or greater than the MEO, the activity remains in‑house.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric threshold is an explicit award criterion used in sealed‑bid competitions under A‑76; it determines whether contracting‑out is allowed when bids are close to the MEO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small‑function (<10 FTE) fair & reasonable price exception
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In functions having less than 10 full‑time equivalents (FTE) ... a cost comparison is not required as long as the price is
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small activities (<10 FTE) agencies may award on the basis of a fair & reasonable price rather than a formal MEO cost comparison; fair & reasonable should be supported by market competition evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to in‑house (recompete) thresholds and approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: To return an activity to in‑house the MEO must better a private offer by a ten percent cost increment (twenty percent lower than the originally competed MEO cost) plus twenty‑five percent of the contractor's capital assets cost; Secretary approval is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High procedural and numeric hurdles make returning contracted activities to Government performance difficult; this standard governs recompete/reinstatement decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary causes of post‑award contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Identified causes: 'increases in the Department of Labor wage determinations, food price increases, added work, and delay in follow‑on contract award.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating post‑award cost growth, examine DOL wage determinations, commodity/food price inflation, contract scope changes/added work, and administrative delays; these are recurring, documented drivers of cost escalation in A‑76 contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and accuracy of management study/PWS/MEO development
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies are 'lengthy ... many times inaccurate and a burden on the activity being studied' and 'an effective study requires advanced planning and preparation, skill, and a comprehensive analysis of the function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of the initial management study (PWS, MEO cost build‑up) is an evaluation dimension — poor studies produce inaccurate MEOs, ambiguous PWSs, and later cost disputes/increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract specification completeness to anticipate added work
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Added work can be anticipated through adequate contract specifications, but usually there is still an additional cost incurred because of unexpected situations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should assess whether solicitations/PWS anticipated routine and foreseeable variability; stronger specifications and explicit scope‑change mechanisms reduce cost growth from added work.

rubrics_metrics.name: COTR selection, training, and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem noted: 'The need for a Contracting Officer's Technical Representative (COTR) who is normally in place for a short duration (2‑3 years), and who receives limited training or experience in quality assurance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective contract administration requires properly trained, experienced, and continuous COTRs; inadequate COTR capacity is a criterion for program weakness and a cause of contract performance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of set‑asides (8(a)/small business) and effect on competition/cost comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Coast Guard A‑76 reviews initially reserved functions for 8(a) small disadvantaged businesses; 'in some commercial activities ... using small businesses in competition may soon be the only option.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserved competitions can bypass formal cost comparisons or change the competitive field; evaluation should record when set‑asides influence whether an A‑76 cost comparison was performed and how that affects value for money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and barriers to returning contracted work in‑house
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Once an activity is contracted‑out, it is extremely difficult to return the effort
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess procedural, financial, and approval barriers (MEO thresholds, asset buy‑backs, Secretary approval) when judging flexibility and long‑term accountability of A‑76 decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program success metrics: cost savings and billet reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured outputs include 'average annual cost savings', number of reviews completed, number contracted‑out vs in‑house, and reduction in military and civilian billets (e.g., table showing reviews, billets reduced, average annual cost savings).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program evaluation should quantify realized fiscal savings and personnel impacts per review/over time, and compare those to expectations and DOD benchmarks (savings per review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptions and workforce impacts (morale, productivity, ratings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems noted: 'The perception that A‑76's purpose is to cut personnel and jobs rather than to have an efficient organization ... Work Force Perception ... Work Force Morale and Productivity ... Affect on Coast Guard Enlisted Ratings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stakeholder perceptions across command levels and track morale/productivity indicators and occupational rating impacts as qualitative program outcomes that affect long‑term effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration practices and planning (follow‑on awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in follow‑on contract award cited as a cause of cost increases; 'adequate advance planning' can prevent some delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contracting offices' timeliness, planning for option years and recompetes, inclusion of cost‑ceiling clauses, and other contract administration mechanisms to control cost growth and maintain continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested contracting controls (cost ceiling clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: MLCPAC suggestion: 'to have a cost ceiling clause incorporated into the contract ... set at a level that would ensure that the contract cost stayed below the MEO cost ... and at least ensure Government cost savings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presence/absence of contractual cost‑ceiling or price‑adjustment provisions as an evaluative criterion for limiting post‑award cost escalation and protecting Government savings.
